The nephew cast a fruitless glance at him as he went towards the door.

“Good night!” said his uncle. “I anticipate the pleasure of seeing you once more in the morning. Sleep well! Show Monsieur my nephew a light to his chamber there!—And set Monsieur my nephew alight in his bed, if you please,” he added privately, before ringing his small bell again and calling his valet to his own bedchamber.

When the valet had attended and withdrawn, Monsieur the Marquis paced about in his loose night-robe, gently making himself ready for sleep on that hot, motionless night. With a rustle about the room, his softly shod feet noiseless upon the floor, he moved like an elegant tiger: looked like an enchanted marquis of the obstinately wicked kind in a tale, whose recurring transformation into a tiger was either just ending or just beginning.

He passed from one end of his luxurious bedroom to the other, revisiting the fragments of that day's journey which presented themselves unsought to his thoughts; the laborious climb at sunset, the sinking sun, the downward road, the mill, the prison upon the crag, the small village in the hollow, the peasants beside the fountain, and the road-mender in his blue cap indicating the chain beneath the carriage. That fountain recalled the fountain in Paris, the small bundle upon the step, the women stooping over it, and the tall man with uplifted arms, crying, “Dead!”

“I am cool at last,” said Monsieur the Marquis, “and can retire to bed.”

Accordingly, leaving a single light alight on the spacious hearth, he dropped his delicate gauze curtains about him, and, as he settled himself to sleep, heard the night interrupt its silence with a long sigh.

For three oppressive hours the stone faces upon the outside walls gazed sightlessly into the dark night; for three oppressive hours the horses rattled their stable racks, the dogs barked, and the owl uttered a sound bearing scarcely any likeness to the sound men-poets commonly allot to owls. Such creatures, however, persist in the obstinate practice of hardly ever speaking the lines written for them.

For three oppressive hours the chateau's stone faces, human and lion, gazed sightlessly into the night. Lifeless darkness covered the whole landscape; lifeless darkness lent its silence to the silencing dust upon every road. The burial-ground had reached a state in which its little mounds of meagre grass could no longer be told apart; for all that could be seen of the figure upon the Cross, it might have descended. Throughout the village, those who levied taxes and those who paid them slept deeply. Dreaming perhaps of feasts, as hungry people commonly do, and of comfort and repose, as the labouring slave and harnessed ox may dream, its gaunt inhabitants slept soundly, nourished and released.

He was handed over to you. You see that I know the circumstances?”

“That is certainly true,” said Defarge. As his wife knitted and sang softly, a seemingly accidental nudge of her elbow had told him that he should answer, but keep his answers short.

“You were the person,” said the spy, “his daughter came to; and she took him from your care to England, accompanied by a tidy gentleman in brown. What was his name? He wore a little wig—Lorry—from Tellson and Company's bank.”

“That is true,” Defarge repeated.

“Such interesting memories!” said the spy. “I have met Doctor Manette and his daughter in England.”

“Have you?” said Defarge.

“You don't hear much about them these days?” the spy asked.

“No,” said Defarge.

“Actually,” madame interrupted, looking up from her knitting and her quiet song, “we hear nothing about them. We had word that they had arrived safely, and perhaps one letter after that, or perhaps two. But since then they have gradually gone their way in life, and we have gone ours. We haven't kept in touch.”

“Quite understandable, madame,” the spy replied. “She is going to marry.”

“Going to?” madame repeated. “She was pretty enough to have married years ago. You English seem cold to me.”

“Oh! You know I'm English.”

“I can hear that your tongue is,” madame answered, “and I assume the man is whatever his tongue is.”

He did not consider this recognition a compliment, but he made the best of it and laughed it off. After finishing his cognac in small sips, he continued:

“Yes, Miss Manette is getting married. But her husband won't be English. Like her, he was born French. And since we were speaking of Gaspard—ah, poor Gaspard! Such cruelty, such cruelty!—it is curious that she will marry the nephew of Monsieur the Marquis, on whose account Gaspard was raised so many feet into the air. In other words, she is marrying the current Marquis. But he lives in England without anyone knowing who he is; he isn't a Marquis there. He is Mr. Charles Darnay. His mother's family name is D'Aulnais.”

Madame Defarge kept knitting steadily, but the news visibly affected her husband. Behind the little counter, however hard he tried as he struck a light and lit his pipe, he could not hide his distress or keep his hand steady. The spy would scarcely have deserved the name if he had failed to notice this and store it in his memory.

Having at least struck this one blow, whatever its value might turn out to be, and with no customers arriving to offer another opportunity, Mr. Barsad paid for his drinks and said goodbye. Before leaving, he took care to remark, with polished courtesy, that he looked forward to the pleasure of seeing Monsieur and Madame Defarge again.

February had begun, and after a month in Bath Anne was becoming increasingly eager for news from Uppercross and Lyme. She wanted to know far more than Mary had told her. Three weeks had passed since she had heard anything at all. All she knew was that Henrietta had returned home and that Louisa, although said to be recovering quickly, remained in Lyme. One evening, while Anne was thinking intently about them all, a letter from Mary arrived, thicker than usual. Adding to her delight and surprise, it came with Admiral and Mrs Croft's regards.

The Crofts must be in Bath! That was something to interest her. Her affection turned towards them quite naturally.

“What's this?” Sir Walter exclaimed. “The Crofts have come to Bath? The Crofts who rent Kellynch? What have they brought you?”

“A letter from Uppercross Cottage, sir.”

“Ah! Letters like that make useful passports. They guarantee an introduction. Still, I would have called on Admiral Croft in any case. I know the courtesies I owe my tenant.”

Anne stopped listening. She could not even have explained how the poor Admiral's complexion escaped comment; the letter absorbed all her attention. Mary had started it several days earlier.

“February 1st.

“My dear Anne,

“I won't apologize for not writing, because I know how little people care about letters in a place like Bath. You must be enjoying yourself far too much to bother about Uppercross, where, as you know very well, there is hardly anything to write about. Our Christmas has been terribly dull; Mr and Mrs Musgrove haven't given a single dinner party throughout the holidays. I don't count the Hayters as anybody. At least the holidays are finally over. I don't believe any children ever had such long ones; I certainly didn't. Yesterday the house emptied, apart from the little Harvilles, though you will be surprised to hear that they have never been home. Mrs Harville must be a strange mother to let them stay away so long. I cannot understand it. I don't think they are at all pleasant children, but Mrs Musgrove seems to like them as much as her grandchildren, if not more. What awful weather we have had! Perhaps you don't notice it in Bath, with your lovely pavements, but it makes a difference in the country. Nobody has visited me since the second week of January except Charles Hayter, who had been coming much more often than anyone wanted. Between ourselves, I think it is a great pity Henrietta didn't stay in Lyme as long as Louisa. It would have kept her away from him for a while.
